chunks: "An active probe has a small amplifier, usually a FET buffer, right at the probe tip.
The amplifier has very high input resistance and very low input capacitance, typically around a picofarad or less, and then drives the cable and the scope's 50 ohm input.
So it loads the circuit far less than a passive probe at high frequency.
The reason that matters is that a passive probe is basically a resistor in parallel with a capacitor of 10 to 15 picofarads. At low frequency it looks like 10 megaohms, great.
But at 100 megahertz that capacitance is only about 130 ohms. If I probe a 500 ohm node, the probe is a real load and slows the edge.
With an active probe at 1 picofarads the reactance at 100 megahertz is 1. 6 kilohms, so the same node barely notices.
So I'd use it for fast digital edges, clocks, high-speed buses, high-impedance nodes and anywhere bandwidth over a few hundred MHz matters.
The price is real: it's more expensive, has a limited input voltage range and DC offset range, adds a bit of noise, needs power from the scope, and is easy to damage with ESD or overvoltage.
For ordinary power rails and slow signals, a passive 10x is better."
